original-commercial-district.html:
The photo was taken from the point where the railroad bridge crosses River Street.  There are fifteen people showing in the picture, seven on the second story of the hotel veranda, one woman, three men, four children, one dog and many, many round-head rocks in the foreground.

   The first building from the left was built in the winter of 1868-69 by F. B. Nichols, who conducted a general store. The next building, in the center of the picture, was the Avenue House. Miner Ball had moved it in from Greenwood. It was run by J. F. Powers, later became Young’s Hotel in 1871, and eventually was known as the Great Northern Hotel. To the right of the hotel was a general store conducted by Frank Hopkins.  The two-story white building on the edge of the clearing was the Chance building.

In the Summer of 1869, Dr. Perry Chance came to what was then known as Crow River, and had built an office, drug store and home on the corner of Railroad avenue and Second street. The streets were barely defined, with no sidewalks and very muddy. He was the first resident physician.  Dr. Perry died November 19, 1871, shortly after establishing himself, leaving his wife to raise five children. After his death, Maranda continued in the druggist business until 1882.

The September 15, 1881 Delano Eagle stated that Mrs. M. A. Chance had kept a drug store for the past 11 years, and did a very fair business, having kept a good stock of drugs always on hand. Besides having a drug store, Mrs. Chance also had charge of the post office, which was kept in the same building. Maranda Chance was appointed postmaster of Delano in 1880, a position she held until 1883, when her son Norman was appointed.

grain-elevators.html: Grain elevators have been central to Delano’s agricultural and commercial life since the community’s earliest days. When the railroad reached Crow River in 1868, plans already called for a 40,000-bushel elevator, and by 1881 the locally organized Delano Elevator Company had constructed its distinctive round elevator, helping make Delano an important regional grain market. The elevator business evolved through different owners and cooperatives, eventually coming under the Styrbicky family, whose Delano Elevator Company expanded into feed grinding and mixing. A devastating fire destroyed the elevator and grinding mill in March 1962, but a modern steel elevator and feed plant was built and opened the following year. The Styrbicky family continued the business until 2011, when Mike “Spike” Persons purchased it and established Spike’s Feed, Seed & Pet Supply, carrying Delano’s grain and feed tradition into a new generation.

In October 1868, the Minneapolis Star Tribune published an article describing the official opening of the St. Paul and Pacific Railroad to Crow River. After describing the trip and the new town, the article stated that the Company would soon build an elevator with a capacity of 40,000 bushels. From the very beginning, having grain elevator was important. Old grain elevators have gone by the wayside in some towns, but not in Delano.

It’s just changed and progressed with the years.

(from The Delano Eagle, September 15, 1881)

“ELEVATORS – There are two wheat buying firms in our village, the Elevator Company and Mr. Louis Rausch. The Delano Elevator Company was organized as a stock company in 1881, and built an elevator with the capacity of 32,000 bushels. The building is an ornament to the town and is already doing a thriving business. Mr. Rausch’s grain house dates back almost as far back as the village, does a very good trade, and has a capacity of 10,000 bushels.”

“Besides his store, Mr. Rausch is proprietor of a grain house, and does a large business in buying wheat and other grain.”

(from The Delano Eagle, December 29, 1881)

DELANO ELEVATOR – The most prominent building both on account of size and the position it occupies in business circles is the new elevator, built the past summer by a stock company with Dittman & Roosen, Chas. Eppel, I. Gutzwiller Jr., John Coolen and John Haffner as stockholders. The elevator has a capacity of 32,000 bushels, and was erected at a cost of $5,000. It is well located on the north side of the railroad track, is supplied with a steam engine, and is doing a very good trade. Since its opening this fall, not less than 25,000 bushels of wheat have been taken in. This addition was needed in Delano, and since its coming it has drawn to our village a great deal of trade from surrounding towns. The prices paid here for wheat have been markedly good from the start, and farmers are confident that in marketing their grain here they are sure of a square deal.”
The round Delano Elevator is shown in the background.

(from the History of Wright County, MN. – Illustrated – 1881)

“A circular elevator, with storing capacity of 32,000 bushels, was built in 1881, and is operated by an engine of fifteen horse-power. It was built by a company formed of citizens of the village, who now control it.”

(from The Delano Eagle, January 1, 1885)

“THE DELANO ELEVATOR COMPANY – Started in business in the spring of 1881, there being at that time no independent elevator in Delano, and erected their round elevator on Railroad Avenue. The company consists of individual merchants and business men of the town who entered into the undertaking with a view to save to the village and its interests the thousands of dollars which the Miller’ Association were yearly taking from the neighborhood farmers and investing elsewhere. The company, since its birth has continued to prosper, and has aided considerably in benefiting the Delano markets. Prior to its opening, the usual quantity of wheat bought here did not exceed 40,000 bushels per year, and often fell short of that amount; now the usual annual market is four times that amount. Besides wheat buying the Elevator Company is engaged in the handling of oats, feed and wood; of the latter several thousands cords were taken in during the past year. Since its opening the elevator has handled 270,000 bushels of wheat, enjoys the widest patronage from wheat growers of any market along this line of road. The Elevator Company consists of I Gutzwiller Jr., President; C. G. Roosen, Secy and Treas.; Chas Eppel, John Coolen, John Haffner. Paid up capital, $7,000; authorized capital, $10,000.”

“RAUSCH’S ELEVATOR – Mr. L. Rausch rents the Landis elevator and is engaged in purchasing wheat for the Minneapolis Millers’ Association. Since harvest his elevator has taken in 45,000 bushels of wheat, and handles each year in the neighborhood of 100,000 bushels. It has a capacity of 8,000 bushels. Louis Rausch has been a resident of Delano since the winter of ’73, and also is the proprietor of another general store, centrally located on Railroad Avenue.”
Sketch from 1898, published in the Delano Eagle

(from The Delano Eagle, December14, 1893)

“GRAIN ELEVATORS – One of the most essential features in the progress and prosperity of a town or country is an excellent grain market, and in this respect, Delano can feel well proud for nowhere on this line of road will be found a more liberal grain market and better facilities for handing it. We have reference to the DELANO ELEVATOR CO., which was organized many years ago, one of its prime movers being I. Gutzwiller Jr., the editor of this paper; the secretary and treasurer of the company is Chas. G. Roosen. The elevator is known all over the county as the Round Elevator of Delano. It has a capacity of 30,000 bushels, and is equipped with the most improved and modern machinery for handling grain cheaply and fast. This is the largest grain elevator and run by the oldest grain firm in the county.”

(from The History of Wright County, Minnesota, Volume II, 1915)

“The old grain house with a capacity of 8,000 bushels was one of the Davidson chain of elevators and was built soon after Delano was founded. It was bought by W. H. Landis and later rented to Louis Rausch. The Delano Elevator Co. was organized May 5, 1881, with a capital stock of $10,000, and the following officers: President, Il Gutzwiller Jr.; secretary and treasurer, C. G. Roosen; trustees, John Coolen, Charles Eppel and John Haffner. The elevator was erected having a capacity of 32,000 bushels.”
William P Moran was the manager at the Delano Farmers Co-operative Elevator Co. in 1921. He moved to Delano from Iona, in Murray County, where he was also had been the manager of a grain elevator.

William was married to Margaret O’Reilly in 1902; they had two daughters, Margaret and Genevieve. After leaving the elevator business, William worked at the school as a janitor and engineer, and later clerked at a hardware store in Delano.

The Delano Elevator had been built as a Farmers’ Cooperative in 1919, but after several years of only partial success it was sold to A. J. Styrbicky and later taken over by his sons Val and Charley.

(from The Delano Eagle Special Edition, 1946)

“Featuring feed grinding and mixing, the Delano Elevator Company was established in 1924. Owned and operated by the Styrbicky Brothers, Charles and Valentine, the business has shown a steady growth and now serves a wide area.”

March 28, 1962 – Flames destroyed the Delano Elevator Co. elevator and grinding mill. The blaze was discovered shortly before 10 pm by John Tischler when he left his office at the Delano Eagle. The Delano volunteer department called for help from Watertown and Maple Plain to help fight the blaze. The fire had engulfed the 60-foot structure when they arrived on the scene, which burned for more than two hours as the firemen fought to keep the flames from spreading to nearby oil storage tanks. Flaming debris covered Great Northern Railway tracks and held up a Willmar-bound passenger train for about an hour, which was then run through on another track. The Minneapolis Star reported that the elevator was owned by Val Styrbicky and his brother-in-law, Sam Gnitka, and that Delano’s Mayor Laurence Rieder estimated the loss at more than $75,000.

On February 23, 1963, The Delano Elevator Company held an Open House, inviting everyone to visit their new modern elevator and feed plant. The new plant is of all steel construction with the most modern equipment for feed grinding and mixing. The Elevator was put together with pre-fabricated steel sections which were lifted in place with a giant crane and welded and bolted together. While the plant was being built Dutch Styrbicky carried on the business as best he could with portable mills operating out of a machine storage shed which had been saved in the fire.

Val “Dutch” Styrbicky continued to run the elevator until he died in 1967. His son Marvin took over and ran it until 2011 when it was bought by Mike “Spike” Persons. His business, Spike’s Feed, Seed & Pet Supply, breathed new life into the old Delano Feed Mill. The business has continued to expand and grow.

great-northern-hotel.html: The Great Northern Hotel was a prominent part of Delano’s early history, serving generations of travelers and salesmen arriving by rail. Its story began in 1868, when Miner Ball moved a small building from the former townsite of Greenwood to Delano and opened it as a hotel. Under James D. Young, it grew into the much larger Young’s Hotel, a three-story landmark capable of accommodating scores of guests and offering a livery stable for travelers continuing to neighboring communities. After operating for a time as the Meister House, John and Magdalena Pfeifer purchased the property in 1901, and in 1902 it became the Great Northern Hotel. Lena Pfeifer continued operating it for decades after her husband’s death. A later fire damaged the third floor, which was subsequently removed, and the building eventually became the Pfeifer Hotel and then an apartment building before being demolished in 1971—ending more than a century of service at this historic Delano site.
In 1858, JD Young purchased the building in Greenwood, MN and moved it to Railroad Ave.
This was the only three story building in Delano.
In 1879, the hotel had expanded to 40 rooms and was considered one of the finest hotels on the rail line.

Many salesmen and other travelers came to the end of the train line and stayed the night. The next morning they would rent livery rigs to travel to outlying towns such as Watertown, Mayer, Lester Prairie and Winsted.

In 1896 a new celebrated drinking fountain (for horses) was installed in front of the Great Northern Hotel by mason Mr. Revolt. It was both attractive and convenient, the city council was congratulated for their good judgement in funding it.

• 1905: The Great Northern Hotel was run by John and Lena Pfeiffer

  • 1915: Lena Pfeiffer was the proprietor

  • 1975: The building fell into disrepair was demolished for the new Delano State Bank

delano-library.html: The Delano Public Library has served the community from several locations since its beginnings in 1930, reflecting both the library’s growth and Delano’s changing downtown. It began in Brown’s Drug Store before moving to the Village Council Chambers in 1940, and by 1952 had a paid librarian. The library joined the Great River Regional Library system in 1969 and subsequently operated from St. Joseph’s Educational Building and, beginning in 1974, the former fire barn on Bridge Avenue, which was renovated by the Crow River Women’s Club. In 2004, the library moved into the former Delano State Bank site, continuing a long tradition of adapting historic community spaces to provide library service to generations of Delano residents.

On November 11, 1939 the first Delano Community Library was opened by the governing board of John F. Tischler, Richard Lebovsky, Mrs. William Sutton and Mrs. Gudrun Greenfield in the Brown’s Drugstore on River street. Gudrun had been a librarian at the University of Minnesota before moving to Delano.

In 1940 the library moved to the village Council Chambers in the City Hall. In 1952 the city passed a mill tax that allowed the private library to become a public one, with a paid librarian. The collection consisted of two walls of books covered with bamboo shades.

In 1969 the Delano library became part of the Great River Regional Library system, a 32-library system encompassing seven counties. Needing more space by then, the library relocated to a room in Handzel Hall, the St. Joseph’s Educational building.

The community library included 80 books that were discards from the Minneapolis Young Quinlan lending library, but deemed in excellent condition. Membership in the community library was $1.

Volunteer librarians included Mrs. R.E. Weller, Mrs. Alfred Strassburger, Mrs E.C. Brown, Mrs. James R. Null, Mrs. J. B. Hills, Mrs C.N. Lundsten, Mrs. Harry Kuka, Mrs. Bert Gilmer, Mrs. Gerhard Von Bank, Mrs. Zwick, Mrs. T. Greenfield and Mrs. William Sutton.

In 1940 the library moved to the village Council Chambers in the City Hall. In 1952 the city passed a mill tax that allowed the private library to become a public one, with a paid librarian. The collection consisted of two walls of books covered with bamboo shades.

In 1969 the Delano library became part of the Great River Regional Library system, a 32-library system encompassing seven counties. Needing more space by then, the library relocated to a room in Handzel Hall, the St. Joseph’s Educational building.

The library soon needed more space again, and 1974 moved back to the Old City Hall, this time in the area that that had once been used as the fire barn. The space was renovated, remodeled and refurnished by the Crow River Federated Women’s Club. It opened on March 8, 1974.

In 1983 the GFWC remodeled the former Council Chambers to add a children’s area, along with new shelving and a check out desk. In 1998 a third room was added for the expanding library.

In 2004 the library moved again, to the former State Bank of Delano on Railroad Avenue, with the help of the City of Delano, the Friends of the Library, and the GFWC. This move gave the library 2,030 square feet of space, and a state-of-the-art library facility.

The library has remained at this location since that time.

eagle-building.html: The Delano Eagle Building at 300 Railroad Avenue represents more than a century of Delano’s newspaper and printing history. The story began in 1872 with the Big Woods Citizen, which soon became the Wright County Eagle and, in 1881, the Delano Eagle. In 1883, a two-story building constructed of locally produced red brick became the newspaper’s permanent home and Delano’s first solid brick building. Its second floor, known as Eagle Hall, also served as an early community entertainment space. In addition to publishing the newspaper, the Eagle Printing Company became known for railroad and commercial printing and operated a highly regarded bookbindery. The Eagle Newspaper and Job Printing Office remained at this Railroad Avenue location for more than 100 years, and its three-building complex was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, preserving the legacy of one of Delano’s oldest and most enduring businesses.

• 1872: A weekly newspaper called the "Big Woods Citizen" was established by Daniel Fish and H.A. Ball. The paper was sold to I. Gutzwiller Jr. and Fran Matchett.

  • 1881: I. Gutzwiller renamed the paper the "Delano Eagle" and the publishing company the "Eagle Printing Company".
The Delano Eagle Newspaper and Printing Office was the home of the oldest established business in Delano.
The first solid two story red brick building in Delano
Besides the newspaper the Eagle Printing Company specialized in railroad and commercial printing. They also operated one of the finest book binderies in Minnesota.
• 1883: A brick was erected as the "Delano Eagle Building". Two addition were added in 1884 and 1885.

• 1979: The three adjacent buildings of the Eagle Newspaper and Printing were added to

    the National Register of Historic Places.
• 1984: Delano Eagle Auction - Complete older print shop sold.
The office operated continuously at its location on Railroad Avenue for over 100 years when it closed in 1984.
• 2019: 300 Railroad Ave is the physical home of Five Technology and J&J Glass and Glazing.

ioof.html:
• Built in 1881 for the C.F. Peters' General Store.

  • The second story served as a hall for the Odd Fellows, Mason, Woodmen, Eastern Star and other lodges.
Look carefully the center building has IOOF letters across the top.

By 1911 the building was known as the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. The Independent Order of Odd Fellows is one of the oldest and largest fraternities in the world. The command of the IOOF is to“visit the sick, relieve the distressed, bury the dead and educate the orphan.”
The building had peep holes in the walls and a bowling alley at one time.
In 1942, the building was cut back from the street and converted to a residence. Unique features of the house are hand cut nails, 12” wood beams instead of 2x4's, and porcelain knobs.

lindsley-bldg.html: The Lindsley Building at 282 Railroad Avenue has been part of Delano’s downtown landscape since 1885, when Joseph Warren Lindsley constructed the handsome two-story brick building to expand his hardware business. Considered one of the finest business blocks in Delano at the time, it featured modern improvements, including an elevator, with the hardware store on the first floor and living quarters above. After leaving the hardware business, Lindsley remodeled the building and opened the Lindsley Hotel in 1909, described as a “thoroughly modern” hostelry. By 1918 it had become known as Packer’s Hotel under James Packer. Although the exact date of its later conversion has not yet been determined, the historic building eventually became apartments and continues to serve as residential housing today.

The elegant building on the corner of Third Avenue and Railroad Avenue was erected in 1885 by Joseph Warren Lindsley to expand his hardware business. He had previously been in the Coolen block on River Street since 1880.

The building was a two story brick, 25 feet front by 70, the lower story being occupied by his hardware store, the upper floor being fitted for a dwelling. It was described as “without a doubt the finest business block in Delano, having been built at a cost of not less than $5,000, and forms a valuable addition to the city’s buildings.”
The building was elegantly finished within, with an elevator and other modern improvements. In 1908 Lindsley decided to quit the hardware business. By 1909 he had opened the Lindsley Hotel...
By 1918, J.W. Lindsley had retired and moved to Minneapolis. The hotel became known as the Packer's. James Packer was listed as the hotel proprietor in 1920.
The building was converted into apartments along the way, which is still how it is used today.

lundsten-lumber.html: Established in 1903 by O.J. Lundsten as the Home Lumber Company and renamed Lundsten Lumber in 1906, the business became one of Delano’s oldest and most enduring family enterprises. Located on Railroad Avenue near the depot, the lumber yard grew into an extensive operation supplying lumber, brick, lime, cement, coal, and other building materials. Management passed from O.J. Lundsten to his nephew Cliff Lundsten and later to Cliff’s son Jim and his wife Ann, while generations of the Lundsten family also played important roles in Delano’s civic and community life. When the family sold the business in 1988, Lundsten Lumber was Delano’s oldest business still under the same family management. The historic building remains in use today as the home of Love INC, preserving a visible connection to more than a century of Delano history.
The Home Lumber Co. was established by O.J. Lundsten in 1903. The name was changed to Lundsten Lumber in 1906.

(from The Great Northwest Magazine, Wright County Edition, December 1909)

THE LUNDSTEN LUMBER CO. – The Lundsten Lumber Co., with headquarters at Delano, are the owners and operators of three lumber yards. Mr. Lundsten established the Home Lumber Co. in 1903, with the help of Andrew Justin, O.W. Lundsten and John Hineman, and in 1906 a change came not only to the name of the firm, but to the owners as well. O.W. Lundsten, who became president of the new firm, is a banker at Hutchison; Geo. A. DuToit, the vice-president, one at Chaska, and O.J. Lundsten, the secretary is a Delano man, having been here a great many years. Of course, it is generally conceded that a company operating several yards has a greater purchasing power than others because of the magnitude of their purchases. The yard here is managed by Mr. O.J. Lundsten, who has been looking after the work practically ever since it first started as the Home Lumber co. Mr. Lundsten is an expert in the lumber line, having long been identified with such work. The yards here are quite extensive and most of the material is under cover. Their office and sheds are a50x70 and 50x80, just opposite the depot, where the firm owns eight 25x100 foot lots. They enjoy the distinction of having the oldest yard in Delano and the largest stock. They carry a very complete line of brick, lime, cement and all grades of coal. When the city cast around for a member of its council and selected O.J. Lundsten, all felt that the choice was wise – now they all know it. He is a gentleman of fine abilities, good judgment and honest purposes.”
Lundsten Lumber Co., 1914. The gentleman in the white shirt in O. J. Lundsten. (from The Delano Eagle Special Edition, 1946)

Lundsten Lumber was the oldest business in Delano under the same family management when it closed. O.J. Lundsten was succeeded by his nephew, Cliff Lundsten. The Lundsten family and the lumber company were deeply tied to Delano's civic life. Cliff Lundsten helped organize Delano’s early community traditions, such as the town's cooperative Santa Claus Day for local children in 1939. Cliff’s son Jim and his wife Ann took over managing the company in the 1950’s, and helped establish local institutions including the Crow River Bank and community planning committees. They sold the business in1988 and retired. Jim and his wife, Ann, were honored as Delano Citizens of the year in 1997.
“The Old Grey Mare, she ain’t what she used to be” - same location, same building, but with a new face.
Today the Lundsten Lumber building is the home of Love INC.

railroad.html: The railroad was central to Delano’s founding and development. When the St. Paul & Pacific Railroad reached the Crow River in 1868, the new settlement grew around its station and depot and was soon named Delano in honor of railroad official F. R. Delano. The Railroad Line The railroad brought passengers, commerce, grain and new businesses, while its bridge across the Crow River and depot became important local landmarks. A new depot was built in 1885, and a new 270-foot railroad bridge followed in 1904, with the bridge undergoing extensive rebuilding in the 1940s. The Railroad Line The Railroad Line The line eventually became part of the Great Northern, Burlington Northern and, today, BNSF Railway. Although Delano’s depot was torn down in 1988, the railroad line and bridge remain enduring reminders of the transportation network that helped create and shape the community. The Railroad Line The Railroad Line

In 1867, the First Division of the St. Paul & Pacific Railroad built 15 miles of line between Minneapolis and Wayzata. The main line was completed and in operation as far as Crow River, October 8, 1868. The post office, established a few weeks later, took the same name. The settlement was called just “the station” or “the depot” for sometime and had been called before that “Eagleville” from the fact that eagle nest were found on the “Island.” Early in the administration of the second postmaster appointment, a meeting was held on the depot platform and it was decided to name the town after F. R. Delano – at that time an official on the railroad.

Mr. Delano had the reputation of being somewhat distant, and as we would say now “grouchy,” and Judge Fish, then a new lawyer, wrote an account of the “christening” for the Pioneer Press. After making a pretty good “story” out of the difficulty in finding a name not already in use, Mr. Fish wound up his article by saying that he thought this selection was safe and bowing to the nature of “the man,” there was “no probability of duplication.” The story was published as joke on Mr. Delano, who fully appreciated it.

By 1868, it was extended another 29 miles to Howard Lake.

October 26, 1868 – the formal opening of the St. Paul & Pacific Railroad to Crow River

“The St. Paul and Pacific Railroad was yesterday opened to Crow River, a point about thirty miles nearly due west from Minneapolis. The first regular train, in charge of conductor H. P. Breed, drawn by the engine Geo. L. Becker, left this city yesterday morning t 10:30, and reached Crow River at 12 o’clock. The officers of the road and a number of prominent gentlemen from Minneapolis and St. Paul, in addition to the regular passengers, took part in the formal opening. At Crow River a large number of people had assembled to witness the arrival of the first train, and as it neared the depot, gave vent to their feelings in loud and enthusiastic cheers. The Company have located the town upon the west bank of the Crow river, and it is certainly not only the most beautiful but the best location for a town west of Minneapolis. Although scarcely two weeks old, it boats of four stores, a hotel, black smith shop, butcher shop, carpenter shop and school house, besides the Railroad buildings, which consist to a large depot, 110 feet in length, a commodious engine house and tank house. The Company will soon build an elevator with a capacity of 40,000 bushels.

At the river the company have built a flume truss bridge 160 feet in length. Beyond the bridge the track is laid about a half a mile, and the track layers are laying at the rate of three quarters of a mile a day.”

(from the Star Tribune (Minneapolis, Minnesota) Tues., Oct. 27, 1868)

Two mixed passenger and freight trains made the round trip daily between St. Paul and Benson by 1870. A special passenger train, the Delano Accommodation, left Delano each morning for St. Paul, made a trip between St. Paul and Minneapolis at noon, and serving immediate stations, returned to Delano at day’s end.

(The Great Northern Railway: A History/ Part 1 1856 to 1916)
Inelegant but perfectly functional coaches were assigned to the Delano Accommodation. (Courtesy of Minnesota Historical Society)

In 1879, this segment of the StP&P was sold to the St. Paul, Minneapolis and Manitoba Railway. The StPM&M had a considerable amount of trackage throughout Minnesota.

By 1890, the StPM&M became part of the Great Northern Railway. The collection of railroads dating back to the St. Paul & Pacific were primarily controlled by railroad magnate James J. Hill.
The Railroad Bridge
A new railroad bridge over the Crow River in Delano was built in 1904, consisting of four girder spans for a total length of 270 feet.

May 26, 1904 – “A crew of about eighty workmen arrived in Delano late Sunday evening and two more crews, each of about the same number, are expected in a short time, and the work of raising the roadbed through the village will soon be commenced. It cannot be definitely found out as those who have the laying our of the work in charge do no seem willing to impart their knowledge to others, but from what little information we could gather, it is probably that the roadbed will be raised, at the bridge, which is the lowest point on the grade, about ten feet, and that the depot site will be changed to a pint on the south side of the track east of Fourth Street. An overhead bridge will be built on River Street, which it is likely that the crossing on Third Street will be graded up. It is hoped that the Company will put up first-class depot, and no doubt they will as the old one has seen better days. When the work opened up earnest there will be “something doing” and time will be quite lively for a couple of months. We understand that the boarding houses will be erected in the eastern part of the village.”

(from the Delano Eagle, Delano, Minnesota)
The bridge was extensively rebuilt between 1945 and 1947, including the replacement of both approaches.

“The Delano Railroad Bridge Is Being Rebuilt and strengthened by a bridge building crew. The extensive work, which is necessary because of a new high-speed train the Great Northern is planning to put on this run, will not be completed until around Christmas time, according to the engineer in charge.

Present plans call for the encasing of the present stone bridge piers and extending the concrete right up to the bottom of the bridge itself. Most of the steel will also be replaced and the west side abutment will be lengthened.

To encase the piers in concrete the workers will have to start work eight feet below the surface of the river. At present a temporary dam is being thrown up around the east pier to shut off the water in preparation for the work to follow.”

(from the Delano Eagle, Delano, Minnesota, June 20, 1946)
2020 Photo
2020 Photo

Currently, the bridge consists of a pair of deck girder spans, a 60 foot deck, a pair of steel stringer spans and a concrete span. The bridge rests on concrete and stone abutments.

By 1970, the Great Northern merged with rival Northern Pacific and Chicago Burlington & Quincy to form Burlington Northern Railroad.

In 1996, BN merged with Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway to form BNSF Railway, the current owners of this line.

(Bridge and Railroad line information from John Marvig and Contributors, 2010-2020)
The Depot
The Delano station was on East Franklin Avenue at South 2nd Street. According to the 1915 GN Valuation Records, a new station was built here in 1885 and was remodeled/expanded in 1904.

Here are excerpts from the Delano Eagle, during the construction of the new depot in 1885:

May 14, 1885 –“ It is amusing to note the rapid steps taken by the railroad company towards building a news passenger depot at this place, and how slowly the structure rises. Two or three times a week some one among the many magnates of the company (and they are all more or less magnates, from General Superintendent down to the tie-men) jumps off while the train stops, takes a tour around the old shanty, looks wise and boards the train again, leaving the wondering public, and expectant employees confident that the coming day will bring a crew of carpenters to commence on the new building. The present system of a sidetracked depot makes it inconvenient for travelers and doubly so for the station employees who are obligated to carry heavy express on their shoulder across he track.”

May 28, 1885 – “It is generally given out that the railroad company have promised a new depot for Delano in the near future, but when, to whom and by whom the news was communicated, we are unable to find out. We will believe in a new depot as soon as we see one commenced, but not before. The song has been sung so frequently that we have tired of the tune, and can’t muster up enough credulity to take stock in a new depot upon everybody’s say-so”.

July 2, 1885 – “Not less than fifty workmen are employed by the railroad company in Delano at the present time, and the work here is being rapidly pushed forward. The lumber for the new depot is being unloaded and piled as fast as it comes in."

July 16, 1885 – “Work still continues upon the new depot, and the structure is fast approaching completion. A gravel crew is at work on Franklin avenue, making room for a sidetrack, and the high bank is fast melting away. The improvement most felt in the new passenger depot promises to be the facility of getting on and off trains, the platform being on the main track instead of as it now is, on a side track. The station men will also bless the new depot’s advent on account of the greater ease in transferring express matter.”

July 23, 1885 – “The new railroad depot at this place is fast nearing completion, and promises when finished to be one of the finest of the railroad buildings west of Minneapolis. The grading of Franklin avenue still continues, the dirt at present taken there from being dumped by the side of the old structure, with a view of filling in the sport the latter now occupies. If the railroad management would only go a step farther and grade Railroad avenue at the intersection of Second street to a level with the track, or with a slight grade, both the village and the railroad management would be mutually benefitted, and the appearance of the new structure enhanced. Burying the old building from the sight of the avenue public, as is now does, looks much like “hiding one’s light under a bushel.””

July 30, 1885 – “The new depot is about finished, lacking at present little more that an outside garment of paint, and is in all respects a credit to the company and the village. The furniture, books, &c. will be moved from the old building, and it removed as soon as circumstances permit. If there were any certainty that the company would act on a suggestion, we would call their attention to an improvement in the matter of platforms. When trains commence to stop at the new depot, a large number will get on and off trains from the north side on account of convenience and saving of time. For the benefit of these a narrow platform, such as seen in many eastern depots, might be set in between tracks the length of the depot, high enough to make the descent from or mounting to the cars easy; such a platform would not interfere in any way, and would be a vast improvement on the old plan.”

August 27, 1885 – “The depot employees moved into their new quarters yesterday, and freight and passenger trains commenced unloading at the new building. The old structure is being dismantled, and will be removed at once.”
The depot employees moved into their new quarters in August of 1885, and freight and passenger trains commenced unloading at the new building. The old structure was dismantled and removed.
Interior of the Depot
Depot Agent

Every depot needed an agent. A.L. Poffenberger was the agent from 1905 until 1932, when he was fatally injured in an accident at the station. Earl Walter was next appointed as the Delano Depot Agent. In 1954 new communication equipment was installed in the depot. Earl’s title had changed to Station Master by then.
Lost Railroad

“One of Delano’s oldest landmarks, the building at one time used by the railroad company as an engine shed, was torn down in 1890 and moved to Willmar. That ancient building was associated with Delano earliest days when the timber of these regions was used for fuel on the locomotives and when that by-gone institution, the wood train, was in all its glory. Some of the oldest conductors in the Northwest associate their start in life with “the old round house up at Delano” and the building was missed by hundreds of passersby who have noticed it for many years. The site was then occupied by the Minneapolis Malting and Brewing Company who erected a large warehouse on the spot.”
The depot was torn down in 1988
The warehouse was torn down in 2026.
Train Collisions
September 25, 1913
Photos by Claudia Beck

Reported in the Delano Eagle: “Two extra freight trains had a rear-end collision on the bridge at River street. The flag man gave the engineer on the second section a signal to come ahead, and he did so. When he found the track was not clear he was unable to stop in time to avoid the collision. The caboose and one box car were smashed, the caboose into kindling wood. Fortunately, no one was in either car. It is certainly a bad place for a wreck, but in this instance none of the cars or the engine left the track. Had they done so they would have gone into the river.”
February 23, 1922

A passenger train and a snow-plow train collided three miles west of Delano on February 23, 1922. The blame for the collision between the east bound passenger train and the heavily ballasted west bound snow plow was placed on the crew of the snow plow train. It was decided that their orders were clear, but that they either mis-read or misunderstood them. The two engines on the passenger train and the snow-plow engine were thrown down a deep embankment into the ditch and the mail car was thrown across the bank on the opposite side. Four of the six men comprising the three engine crews were killed – probably instantly and the fifth man died before the rescuers could ger him to the hospital in Montrose. Several were injured more or less seriously and were taken to the cities on a train sent out for there immediately, and to which the passengers were all transferred. It was bitterly cold, and the snow piled along the track by the snow plow which had made one trip over the road after the storm, but the passengers made the best of it and were surprisingly calm. Trains were delayed about twenty-four hours. It is understood that the crew on the snow plow had realized their mistake, stopped their train, and intended to back into Delano when the collision took place. If the snow-plow train had been under way it would have plowed its way through the passenger train. (from the March 2, 1922 Delano Eagle)

A week after the collision the three engines which were destroyed in the fatal wreck had all been raised and are shown standing on the track north of the depot in Delano, awaiting removal to the shops. One of the engines still had fire in the fire box when brought in.

Kathy Gow wrote this story about the collision and her dad:

“On Thursday, February 23, 1922, my dad, Lauren Horsch, who was almost 13 years old, went to the well to get a pail of water on the farm where he lived with his parents, Andrew and Margaret Horsch and his brothers and sisters. It was 4:40 p.m. He heard a train whistle from the east and another train whistle from the west. He saw the two trains collide. Somehow he ran down to the railroad track which was located quite some way north of the house. His dog went with him. Passengers were on one of the trains and there were a lot of neighbors who came to see the accident. Four of the six train crew died instantly, scaled to death by the steam. Another crew member dies before he could be taken to Montrose. When my dad returned later to his house he had to wrap his dog in a blanket in the barn because he was cold and shivering.”

dwright-county-bank-bldg.html:
Timeline:

1868-69 – F.B. Nichols built a store on Railroad Avenue between the current 2nd and 3rd streets. He opened a general store, and was the second postmaster of Delano.

1873 – F. B. Nichols sold the building and stock of goods to Row Brasie.

1880 – Wright County Bank founded by C M. Dittman and C. G. Roosen in building bought from Row Brasie

1882 – Roosen bought out Dittman, and continued the business as a private bank

1884 – Wright County Bank of Delano incorporated, in new building at 204 Railroad Ave.

1893 – Wright County Bank is still located at 204 Railroad Avenue

1910 – Wright County Bank is now located at 220 River Street

1910 – The Wright County Bank and the State Bank of Delano merged, and located in the building at 115 Bridge Avenue E.

2019 – the building at 204 Railroad Avenue is currently used for apartments

In August, 1880, C.M. Dittman, of Farmington, and C.G. Roosen, of St. Paul, visited a number of places in Wright County with a view of engaging in the banking business. They finally decided upon Delano, bought the Brasie building and lots, and on October 1, 1880, opened the Wright County Bank. By 1881, the bank was considered to be prominent among the business institutions of Delano. Dittman and Roosen were doing an extensive business, and about to establish themselves in new and elegant quarters. Roosen bought out Dittman in 1882, and continued the business as a private bank. He incorporated as the Wright County Bank is 1884, and it was about this time that the building at 204 Railroad Avenue was built. The building was described in 1893 as a large, two-story brick building, with a large fireproof brick vault, within which is an all steel safe held shut by a time lock. In 1910 the Wright County Bank and the State Bank of Delano, which had incorporated in 1908, merged, and continued in the State Bank building at 115 Bridge Avenue E.
The elegant brick building on the corner of 2nd Street and Railroad Avenue is used as apartments today.
